reason: Of a person, current 'stout' chiefly means portly, so a typical reader has Athena make Odysseus fatter while she 'beautifies' him for athletic trials. Butler's sense is strong and solidly built (Greek passona, 'thicker, sturdier', Od. 8.20). 'Sturdier' keeps his meaning and his comparative. 'Stout' stays where it is current, in 'good stout clothing' at 7.21; that split by referent is to be recorded.

old: I will find you in everything.
new: I will supply you with everything.
reason: An obsolete sense of 'find': to supply someone with something, as in 'all found'. Current English reads it as 'I will come and find you', or cannot read it, and the reader had to guess. The sense matters, because the king is undertaking to provide the feast (Greek pasi parexo, Od. 8.39, 'I will provide for all'). 'Supply ... with' is the plain current verb for Butler's sense. The change also removes a second, different 'find' from a paragraph that opens with 'has found his way'.

old: and Alcinous killed them a dozen sheep
new: and for them Alcinous killed a dozen sheep
reason: An indirect object without 'for' after 'killed' is obsolete. Coming straight after 'crowds of men ... both old and young', it first reads as the king killing the crowd, the kind of syntax that hides who is done to. Moving 'them' into a 'for' phrase at the head of the clause (the Greek order, toisin d' Alkinoos, Od. 8.59) keeps every word and leaves the list intact.

'In practice' is now a fixed idiom for 'in reality', so the qualifier reads as nonsense or as a hedge. Butler means when the Achaeans were practising archery (Greek hote toxazoimeth' Achaioi, Od. 8.220, 'when we Achaeans shot'). 'At practice' keeps Butler's noun and changes only the preposition. 'Before Troy' (= at the siege) was decoded and is kept, here and at 8.49.

old: I can throw a dart farther
new: I can throw a spear farther
reason: Current 'dart' is the small missile of the pub game, which makes the boast absurd. Butler's 'dart' is the old word for a light spear (Greek douri akontizo, Od. 8.229, 'I hurl a spear'). 'Spear' is the plain current word for the object, and the object itself is kept.

old: Let us go to the couch of Hephaestus
new: Let us go to the bed of Hephaestus
reason: To a present-day reader a couch is a sofa. The lay turns on the bed that Hephaestus has netted with chains ('marriage bed', 'bedposts', 'all over the bed', 8.18). If the lovers go to a 'couch', the trap they fall into is on the wrong piece of furniture. Butler's couch is that bed (Greek lektronde, Od. 8.292). Accepted Book 3 made the same change ('Nestor left his couch' → 'left his bed', 3.31); Dawn's formulaic couch at 5.0 is a different case and stays. Apply together with B08-08 or not at all.

new: She was not at all reluctant
reason: 'Nothing loath' (Butler: 'nothing loth') is dead in this construction; GLOSSARY lists it for replacement, and read as 'loathe' it blurs whether Aphrodite consents, which is the point of the lay. 'Not at all reluctant' is the literal modernization (nothing → not at all, loth → reluctant) and keeps Butler's understatement. Why not the edition's 'readily enough' (3.36 ×2, 15.15)? It is an adverb and cannot follow 'She was'. The collision given in the adjudication was wrong, as independent verification R1 noted: Butler's ¶20 has no 'willing', 'readily' or 'enough'.

The companion of B08-06, in the sentence where the trap springs. Butler's 'couch' here renders demnia, the same Greek word as his 'bed' at 8.21 ('asleep on my bed'). Apply together with B08-06 or not at all.

'Toils' in the sense of a net or snare is dead outside the literary idiom 'in the toils of'. The current 'toils' (labors) makes 'caught in the toils ... spread for them' momentarily unreadable. 'Net' names Butler's object, the chains hung 'like cobwebs' (8.18) and spread over the bed. Accepted Book 4 made exactly this change ('a lioness caught in the toils' → 'caught in a net', 4.72).

The sense of 'baggage' as a disreputable woman is obsolete. Today the word means luggage or 'emotional baggage', so the insult blurs into 'burdensome'. What Hephaestus says is that his wife is shameless (Greek kunopidos, Od. 8.319, 'dog-eyed', i.e. shameless). 'Hussy' is the current, if dated, word for exactly Butler's sense. It keeps his 'his X of a daughter' construction and his comic, bitter register.

old: He had done so before an upper servant told him
new: He had done so by the time an upper servant told him
reason: Straight after 'a knot that Circe had taught him', 'He had done so before' reads first as the idiom 'on earlier occasions'. This garden path hides the sequence Butler states: the knot was finished, then came the call to the bath. 'By the time' states Butler's relation exactly (he had finished when he was called) and adds nothing. It does not reintroduce v1's 'hardly', which round 1 removed as a change of sense (Book 8 continuity §5b, B08-P042 = p41).
